opus-5.5.text:
Well, first, I should say that nobody outside OpenAI really knows, because they've been quite cagey about it. So what I can give you is my speculation, the account that would make the behavior I see make sense to me.

I think of o1 as an LLM with something like AlphaGo bolted on top of it. With the standard LLM, you have this autoregressive model trained on web-scale data, and it's essentially doing System 1, approximate retrieval. It just completes the prompt. The big problem with that is there's no guarantee that what it produces is correct, and the computation it spends is basically the same whether you ask it a trivial question or an NP-hard planning problem. That alone tells you it can't really be reasoning in any principled sense.

What o1 seems to do differently is two things. First, it spends inference-time compute that scales with the problem. Second, and more interesting, I think there's a reinforcement learning phase in the pre-deployment stage. Imagine you treat the generation of intermediate tokens, what people like to call the "chain of thought," as actions. Think of them less as thoughts and more as moves in a game, like prompt augmentations. You start with a problem, you generate a sequence of these pseudo-actions, and at the end you check the answer with a verifier. That's possible for things like math, code, and planning problems where you can generate synthetic data and check correctness. Then you do RL, much like AlphaGo learns which moves lead to wins, to learn a policy for which sequences of intermediate tokens tend to lead to correct answers. Over many problems you learn Q-values for these augmentations.

At inference time, the model then uses that learned policy, perhaps with some search like rollouts, to generate a long sequence of these tokens before committing to an answer. That would explain why it takes so long, why you get charged for all these hidden "reasoning tokens" you never get to see, and why the cost varies with the problem.

Under that account, what it's doing isn't simply autoregressive completion anymore. I'd call it a large reasoning model rather than a large language model. And that's consistent with what we actually saw when we tested it on PlanBench. On Blocksworld, the standard LLMs had been stuck. Even the best ones did pretty poorly, and on obfuscated versions like Mystery Blocksworld they collapsed to near zero. o1-preview did substantially better, which no pure autoregressive LLM had done. So something qualitatively different is going on.

But I want to be careful. It still isn't sound. It doesn't come with guarantees. Its performance degrades as problems get longer, it will confidently tell you unsolvable problems are solvable, and it can be quite expensive compared to a classical planner like Fast Downward that solves these instances essentially instantly and correctly. And one more caution: the intermediate tokens shouldn't be anthropomorphized as the model's "thinking." Their semantics doesn't really matter. What matters is whether, after RL, they help get you to a verifiably correct answer. So my view is: put it in an LLM-Modulo kind of framework, with external verifiers, if you actually care about correctness.

r001.rationale: It hypothesizes an RL phase that treats intermediate-token prompt augmentations as moves and learns which sequences lead to correct answers.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the LLM’s context window as analogous to a board position.

r003.rationale: It describes intermediate tokens or prompt augmentations as the learned actions, rather than actions in the problem’s domain.

r004.rationale: It says a verifier checks the answer at the end and RL learns which sequences of earlier augmentations tend to lead to correct answers.

r005.rationale: It mentions generating and checking synthetic data, but does not propose using systematic solvers to create problems with known answers.

r006.rationale: It mentions learning Q-values, but does not explain that updating the language model’s weights implicitly approximates them.

r007.rationale: It mentions possible search or rollouts at inference time, but does not propose Monte Carlo tree search to improve learned Q-value estimates.

r008.rationale: It does not use a stone-soup analogy or question the model’s credit for reasoning enabled by added mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that I don't actually know how o1 works, and I think that's partly the point. OpenAI has been quite deliberately opaque about it. They tell us there's a "chain of thought" that the model produces before it answers, and they tell us it's trained with reinforcement learning, and then they hide the actual chain of thought from users. So we're left to reverse-engineer from the outside.

But if you ask me what account would make the behavior make sense, I think it's something like this. Take a base LLM, which, as I've argued for a long time, is essentially an approximate retrieval engine. It's very good at producing plausible-looking continuations, including plausible-looking reasoning traces, but it has no guarantee that any of those traces are correct. Now, what you can do is move from the one-shot setting to a generate-and-test or search-like setting. You let the model generate many candidate "thought" sequences, you have some verifier, maybe for math and code it's an actual checker, maybe elsewhere it's a learned reward model, and then you use reinforcement learning to push the model toward producing the kinds of intermediate token sequences that tend to lead to verified correct answers.

So in my view o1 is not an LLM in the old sense. It's an LLM plus an RL-trained policy over what we might loosely call "reasoning tokens," plus a lot of inference-time compute. That's actually closer to the kind of thing we've been talking about with LLM-Modulo frameworks, where the LLM is the idea generator and something else is doing the verification. The difference is that OpenAI seems to have internalized some of that search into the model through training, rather than keeping an explicit external verifier at inference time. And that's why it feels different from GPT-4 with a "let's think step by step" prompt. It's not just prompting; it's a changed training objective.

What this account also explains is the pattern of results. The improvements are dramatic in domains where you can get reliable reward signals, like competition math and coding, and much more modest elsewhere. If the magic were some new general reasoning capability, you wouldn't expect that lopsidedness. If it's RL against verifiable targets, you'd expect exactly that. It also explains why it's expensive at inference time, and why the chain of thought they show you is a cleaned-up summary rather than the real thing. The real thing is probably full of backtracking and dead ends, because that's what search looks like.

Now, what I would still resist is the claim that this makes the system a "reasoner" in the sense a planning person would mean. The RL doesn't give you guarantees. It gives you a better-calibrated heuristic for generating candidate solutions. Where there's a verifier in the loop, that's fine. Where there isn't, you're back to trusting the model's own judgment, and we have plenty of evidence that these models are not reliable self-verifiers. So my account is: o1 is approximate retrieval, plus learned search behavior, plus test-time compute, and its competence tracks exactly how good the verification signal was during training. That makes the capabilities make sense to me, and also the limitations.

astra-6.text:
The account that would make sense to me is that you have a language model generating candidate reasoning steps, some mechanism for evaluating those steps or their consequences, and additional computation at inference time to explore alternatives. That gives you a way to improve over simply producing the first answer that comes to mind.

But the crucial question is: where does the evaluation come from? Generating something that looks like a chain of reasoning is not the same as establishing that the reasoning is correct. If the model proposes a solution and an external verifier checks it—say, by executing code or checking mathematical constraints—then I have a fairly clear account of why the system can become more reliable. This is the kind of architecture I call an LLM-modulo framework: the language model proposes, and the appropriate verifiers constrain what gets accepted.

You can also train the model using feedback from verifiable tasks, so that it becomes better at proposing useful steps and correcting mistakes. That could explain substantial improvements even when you don't have an external verifier at deployment. But a learned ability to predict which answers will pass verification is still different from verification itself.

So I would find an account involving reinforcement learning, additional inference-time computation, and some form of search and evaluation quite plausible. I wouldn't claim that this establishes exactly what OpenAI is doing internally. And I would want to know how well the improvement transfers to problems where correctness is difficult to check. That's where the distinction between producing plausible reasoning and producing reliable reasoning becomes especially important.

sol-6.1.text:
The account that would make sense to me is that they have taken a language model and used reinforcement learning to make it generate intermediate steps that improve its chances of getting the final answer right. And then they give it more computation at inference time to do that. That is a plausible way to get better performance. But it leaves a very important question: what is checking those intermediate steps?

In a domain like mathematics or programming, you may have an external verifier—a proof checker, or tests you can run. Then you have a very interesting architecture: the language model proposes candidates, the verifier provides feedback, and you use that feedback to search for a better candidate. The language model need not itself be a sound reasoner for that overall system to solve reasoning problems.

If, instead, the model is generating a longer chain of thought and evaluating it using its own learned judgments, that can still improve results. But generating something that looks like deliberation does not, by itself, establish that the steps are valid. You have to distinguish an increased probability of a correct answer from a guarantee of correctness.

So I would want to know where the feedback comes from, what is being verified, and how the additional computation is being used. That would make the capabilities intelligible to me much more than simply saying that the model has learned to think.
